A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CHaRS research. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: V1 reports original jailbreaking, toxicity-mitigation, and image-style experiments, plus clustering and principal-component analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds original human-preference, perceptual-similarity, coupling, covariance, and throughput results.

M1.justification: The default CHaRS and CHaRS-PCT procedures remain unchanged. New Appendix E.6 introduces and evaluates a diagonal-covariance variant with affine component maps and piecewise steering-strength behavior, defined in Eqs. (29)–(30). The normalization clarification in Remark 3.2 already appeared in v1's implementation appendix.

E1.justification: The represented datasets and tasks remain unchanged, including ADVBENCH/ALPACA, RealToxicityPrompts, language-utility benchmarks, and COCO-based cyberpunk and sketch generation. Sketch already appeared in v1's appendix. Human ratings, LPIPS, and throughput measurements assess retained coverage rather than introducing a new model task or input domain.

E2.justification: V2 adds nearest-neighbor and uniform coupling as evaluated alternatives to OT coupling in Section 5 and Table 5. The main ActAdd, DirAbl, and Linear-AcT comparisons are retained. ACT is newly discussed as related work but is not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: V2 substantially expands evaluation procedures: a 44-participant two-alternative forced-choice study, LPIPS against style reference images, coupling comparisons at fixed K and over K=2–15, and throughput measurements on 100 harmless and 104 harmful prompts. These are new protocols; the original benchmark splits and evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cluster-count and principal-component ablations, v2 tests whether OT matching outperforms alternative couplings, whether independently estimated diagonal covariances help, and whether CHaRS adds inference overhead. Section 5 and Appendices E.6–E.7 therefore add substantive tests of central design choices and computational efficiency.

E5.justification: V2 explicitly reports standard deviations for human preferences and LPIPS in Tables 4 and 8 and explains shared variance for complementary binary preferences. V1's Table 3 already contained uncertainty values, which remain unchanged. No new seed counts or repeated-run counts are disclosed, and the new uncertainty calculations are not fully specified.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their values. New results include CHaRS style preferences of 54.32% for cyberpunk and 78.94% for sketch, LPIPS of 0.67/0.69 versus Linear-AcT's 0.70/0.74, and tuned coupling ASRs of 95.19% for OT, 94.23% for nearest neighbor, and 87.50% for uniform coupling. Further results show lower ASR with diagonal covariances and throughput close to ActAdd. Section 4.2 also corrects the maximum zero-shot toxicity reduction from 38% to 42% and attributes the approximately 43% CLS reduction to Qwen2.5-7B.

T1.justification: V2 corrects the Gaussian transport matrix accompanying Eq. (2) and an inverse exponent in the equal-covariance proof. Section 3.2 replaces isotropy alone with equal paired covariances as the justification for translation. Appendix E.6 adds the diagonal-covariance map and its geodesic interpretation; the main mixture-OT derivations and PCT rank argument are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract broadens its characterization of DiM from transport between equal-covariance unimodal Gaussians to distributions differing in their first moments. The principal CHaRS/PCT contributions and claims of improved behavioral control remain unchanged; the additional experiments mainly support existing claims.

C2.justification: V2 adds a possible limited-sample explanation for the diagonal-covariance variant's poorer performance and updates the corresponding limitation. Appendix E.7 interprets the throughput results as minimal additional overhead while explicitly qualifying comparisons with unsteered models because refusal responses are shorter.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, specifies vLLM and a single NVIDIA H100 for the new throughput study, and explains estimation of diagonal covariances from cluster-assigned activations. It also clarifies which layer's centroids and coupling are used for directional ablation. These supplement the retained implementation details.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wang et al.'s ACT and distinguishes its paired-data requirements and per-cluster steering from CHaRS's unpaired matching and position-dependent field. Talamon et al. and Langley references are removed. Other title, year, and publication-detail updates largely concern the same cited works.

P1.justification: Related Work moves from Appendix B to main-text Section 6, with corresponding appendix renumbering. V2 adds acknowledgements and makes localized edits to the abstract, explanations, results discussion, and limitations. Most existing prose and the overall methodological narrative are retained.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands the result displays with six new tables covering human preferences, coupling strategies, LPIPS, covariance configurations, and throughput. Existing figures are retained, with relocations such as Figures 4–5 moving to page 9. The notation table and appendix material also move, while the established visual style remains.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens validation through human and perceptual checks beyond v1's CLIP-based assessment, direct coupling/covariance controls, and measured inference overhead. Mathematical corrections and code-access information also help. The gains remain bounded: the new mechanism tests cover one LLM, human-study uncertainty is incompletely documented, and Appendix Eq. (20) still conflicts with the corrected Gaussian transport formula.
